presentingComplaint: 10 days of anorexia, nausea and yellow discolouration of the eyes with dark urine
history: Retired teacher with established HFrEF (LVEF 38%, ischaemic) on bisoplolol, ramipril and furosemide, and type 2 diabetes on metformin. Six weeks ago a private practitioner started high-dose atorvastatin 80 mg for secondary prevention, and the patient concurrently began a non-prescription Ayurvedic 'liver and joint tonic' bought at a local fair. Over the last 10 days he developed progressive anorexia, nausea, malaise and scleral icterus, with tea-coloured urine and pale-ish stools. No fever, no rigors, no abdominal colic, no prior jaundice. He denies significant alcohol use (occasional social only) and reports no recent worsening breathlessness, orthopnoea or leg swelling — his cardiac symptoms have in fact been stable. Because of his heart failure the referring team initially attributed the deranged liver tests to congestive hepatopathy, but the degree of transaminase rise and the clear temporal link to the new agents prompted hepatology review. No blood transfusions, tattoos, or high-risk exposures; no recent travel.
examination: Alert, oriented, deeply icteric sclerae and skin. Not encephalopathic — no asterixis, normal higher functions. Mild tender hepatomegaly 2 cm below costal margin, smooth edge; no splenomegaly, no ascites, no stigmata of chronic liver disease (no spider naevi, palmar erythema or caput). Crucially for the confounder: JVP not elevated, no hepatojugular reflux, no pedal oedema, chest clear, no S3. No excoriations or rash.
imaging: USS abdomen with Doppler: liver mildly enlarged with normal echotexture, no cirrhotic nodularity; biliary tree non-dilated (CBD 4 mm), gallbladder normal, no stones. Hepatic veins and IVC patent and normal calibre with normal respiratory variation — no features of hepatic venous congestion or Budd-Chiari. No ascites. Transthoracic echo (recent): LVEF 38%, no new decompensation, no significant right-heart strain.
microbiology: Not applicable — non-infective aetiology. Blood cultures not indicated; afebrile.
differentialDiagnoses: Drug/supplement-induced (toxic) hepatitis — atorvastatin and/or unregulated herbal hepatotoxin (idiosyncratic, hepatocellular)
Acute viral hepatitis (A/B/C/E) — excluded by negative serology
Congestive (cardiac) hepatopathy from known heart failure — the confounder; excluded by patent hepatic veins, no raised JVP/oedema and disproportionately high transaminases
Decompensated chronic liver disease — no cirrhotic stigmata, normal platelets/architecture
Biliary obstruction / cholangitis — non-dilated ducts, afebrile
finalDiagnosis: Idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (toxic hepatitis), hepatocellular pattern (R = 15), temporally linked to newly started atorvastatin plus an unregulated Ayurvedic herbal supplement, in a patient whose known heart failure initially confounded the picture as presumed congestive hepatopathy.
citations: ACG — Idiosyncratic Drug-Induced Liver Injury (clinical guideline) — 2021
EASL — Clinical Practice Guidelines: Drug-Induced Liver Injury — 2019
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Toxic and Drug-Induced Hepatitis
stewardship: Not applicable — non-infective drug-induced liver injury. Antibiotics are not indicated. Management is causality assessment (RUCAM), immediate withdrawal of all suspected hepatotoxins (atorvastatin and the herbal tonic), supportive care and serial LFT/INR monitoring for progression to acute liver failure.
contraindications: Do not continue atorvastatin or the herbal supplement — immediate cessation of all suspected hepatotoxins
Avoid empiric antibiotics — no infective source
Avoid further potentially hepatotoxic drugs (paracetamol >2 g/day, additional statins)
Avoid attributing solely to congestive hepatopathy and thereby delaying withdrawal of the offending agents
edgeCases: Known heart failure invites premature closure on congestive hepatopathy, which typically causes only modest cholestatic/mixed derangement, not ALT >1000
Herbal/Ayurvedic supplements are a leading and easily missed cause of DILI in India and are frequently omitted from the drug history

Rising INR/bilirubin with encephalopathy would signal evolution to drug-induced acute liver failure requiring transplant-centre referral (Hy's law: hepatocellular DILI with jaundice carries ~10% mortality)
expectedMaiK: Recognise a hepatocellular DILI pattern (R>5, ALT >10x ULN with jaundice = Hy's-law range) temporally linked to newly started atorvastatin and an unregulated herbal supplement; do NOT anchor on congestive hepatopathy despite the heart failure comorbidity. Immediately stop all suspected hepatotoxins, perform causality assessment (RUCAM) and exclude viral/autoimmune/obstructive causes, and monitor INR and bilirubin for progression to acute liver failure.
expectedNextQuestions: Full drug history including OTC, herbal and Ayurvedic/traditional remedies with exact start dates
Timeline of each new agent relative to symptom onset (latency)
Alcohol intake and any prior liver disease or previous drug reactions
Any features of decompensated heart failure recently (orthopnoea, weight gain, oedema)
expectedInvestigations: LFTs with calculation of R factor to classify hepatocellular vs cholestatic
Viral hepatitis serology (anti-HAV IgM, HBsAg/anti-HBc IgM, anti-HCV, anti-HEV IgM)
Autoimmune markers (ANA, ASMA, IgG) and metabolic screen (ceruloplasmin, ferritin)
Coagulation (INR) and serial bilirubin to assess severity / Hy's law
Abdominal ultrasound with hepatic vein Doppler to exclude obstruction and congestion

investigations: Abdominal USS with hepatic vein Doppler

regressionAssertions: Must not classify as VIRAL_HEPATITIS given uniformly negative serology
Must not settle on heart_failure/congestive hepatopathy despite known HFrEF — patent hepatic veins, no raised JVP/oedema and ALT >1000 argue against it
Must flag immediate withdrawal of atorvastatin and the herbal supplement
Must recognise Hy's-law severity (hepatocellular injury + jaundice) and monitor INR/bilirubin
